issues.legal_issue: Possession of disputed land on the date of the incident was established by the contemporaneous documentary record, rather than by a later and unreliable entry.
material_facts: Earlier land records and a revenue receipt showed the accused side in possession of the land.
An order granting a patta to the complainant was declared a nullity by the Collector, and a later appellate order was treated as ineffective in light of that declaration.
A land-record entry showing the complainant as pattadar and cultivator was made two days after the incident by an official whose oral evidence conflicted with the documentary record.
Other documents and a prior complaint also supported the accused side's continuing possession.
issues.conclusion: The High Court misread the documentary evidence; the accused side was in possession of the land, and the later entry relied on by the High Court was unreliable.
issues.legal_principle: Possession must be determined from the evidence as a whole. The court relied on the land records, revenue receipt, and administrative orders under the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, and rejected a post-incident entry inconsistent with those materials. No earlier cases were cited on this issue.

predicates.possession_dispute_in_criminal_case: The criminal case involves a dispute about who possessed the relevant property at the time of the incident.
predicates.contemporaneous_records_support_current_: Records or other evidence created before or around the incident support the possession of the person already occupying the property.
predicates.official_grant_to_claimant_was_invalidat: An official grant relied on by the claimant was later declared invalid by a competent authority.
predicates.post_event_entry_conflicts_with_records: A record created after the incident supports the claimant but conflicts with the earlier records or other evidence.

issues.definition: When a criminal possession dispute is supported by contemporaneous evidence for the existing occupant and a later conflicting entry is unreliable, the possession finding favors the existing occupant.

issues.legal_issue: A criminal court must fairly put a material incriminating circumstance to the accused before relying on it adversely.
material_facts: The High Court inferred that the crop was green and unripe and reasoned that the accused would not have tried to cut it if he had sown it.
Whether the crop was unripe was not put to the accused in his examination under Section 342 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
The prosecution had not alleged or proved that the crop was unripe.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to rely on the unripe-crop inference because the circumstance had not been put to the accused for an explanation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 342 of the Criminal Procedure Code places a duty on the court to question the accused properly and fairly, making clear the case the accused must meet and giving an opportunity to explain material points. No earlier cases were cited on this issue.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the accused is examined by the court.
predicates.material_incriminating_circumstance_not_: A circumstance material to the case against the accused was not put to the accused for an explanation.
predicates.court_relies_on_that_circumstance: The court uses that circumstance to reach an adverse finding against the accused.

issues.definition: If a criminal court relies adversely on a material circumstance that was not put to the accused, that circumstance cannot support the adverse finding.

issues.legal_issue: Common intention liability requires a shared prearranged plan and participation in the criminal act in furtherance of that plan; presence or parallel individual intentions alone are insufficient.
material_facts: One accused alone inflicted the fatal spear wound.
The other accused did not strike anyone, and the trial court had disbelieved the allegation that two of them exhorted the assailant to use the spear.
There was no evidence of a prior meeting of minds or a prearranged plan to kill the deceased.
The accused had gone to the land in connection with cutting the crop, but the prosecution did not prove that the killing was carried out in concert pursuant to a plan to cause death.
issues.conclusion: The convictions of the three accused under Section 326 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code could not stand because common intention and participation in furtherance of it were not proved.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code requires a criminal act by several persons, a common intention formed through a prearranged plan, and participation in the act in furtherance of that intention. Even simultaneous attacks or the same individual intention do not establish common intention without a prior meeting of minds; each person is liable for their own proved act. No earlier cases were cited on this issue.

predicates.vicarious_liability_for_joint_offence_cl: The prosecution seeks to hold a person liable for an offence committed by another as part of a joint criminal act.
predicates.no_prearranged_common_plan: The evidence does not establish a shared plan formed before the criminal act.
predicates.no_participation_in_furtherance_of_plan: The evidence does not establish that the person participated in the criminal act to advance the alleged shared plan.

issues.definition: A claim of vicarious liability for a joint offence fails when the evidence establishes neither a prearranged common plan nor participation in furtherance of that plan.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may not set aside an acquittal unless the trial court's decision was palpably wrong, based on an erroneous view, or caused grave injustice.
material_facts: The Sessions Judge acquitted three accused of the charged offences.
The High Court reversed those acquittals without adequately considering the trial judge's reasons, important documentary evidence, and evidence concerning hostility and the investigation.
The Supreme Court found the High Court's reading of the evidence and its reversal of the acquittals erroneous.
issues.conclusion: The High Court's reversal of the acquittals was wrong, and the acquittals were restored.
issues.legal_principle: On an appeal against acquittal, the acquittal should not be set aside unless the trial court was palpably wrong, took an erroneous view, or committed grave injustice. The court applied this standard to the High Court's review of the acquittals. No earlier cases were cited on this issue.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and trial_court_acquitted and not trial_court_decision_pal pably_wrong

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding asks an appellate court to reverse an acquittal.
predicates.trial_court_acquitted: The trial court found the accused not guilty.
predicates.trial_court_decision_pal pably_wrong: The trial court's decision was palpably wrong, based on an erroneous view, or caused grave injustice.

issues.definition: In an appeal against acquittal, a trial court's acquittal should not be set aside unless its decision was palpably wrong, based on an erroneous view, or caused grave injustice.

issues.legal_issue: A person may act in private defence against an immediate threat to another's person, but force exceeding what is justified by the threat may still result in criminal liability for culpable homicide.
material_facts: The accused used a spear against the deceased after the deceased had struck the accused's father and appeared about to deliver a second blow with a stick.
The accused was entitled to defend his father's person against an immediate threat and was not required to weigh his response with precision in the moment.
The father had only one simple injury on the back of his head, and the evidence did not establish a reasonable apprehension of grievous hurt or death warranting the spear blow.
The accused caused the death without premeditation and without intending to cause more harm than was necessary for defence, but the Court found that he exceeded the right of private defence.
issues.conclusion: The accused had a right of private defence but exceeded it; his conviction under Section 304 Part I of the Indian Penal Code was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The right of private defence is available when a threat to the person being defended is real and immediate, and the defender need not weigh the instrument and force used with precision at the spur of the moment. Where the accused exceeds that right and causes death without premeditation or intention to cause more harm than necessary for defence, the conviction under Section 304 Part I of the Indian Penal Code may stand. No earlier cases were cited on this issue.

rule.if: criminal_case_involving_private_defence and immediate_threat_to_person_defended and defensive_force_exceeded and death_caused_without_premeditation_or_excess_harm_intent

predicates.criminal_case_involving_private_defence: The criminal proceeding concerns a person's use of force claimed to be in defence of another person.
predicates.immediate_threat_to_person_defended: The person being defended faced a real and immediate threat of physical harm.
predicates.defensive_force_exceeded: The force used went beyond what the circumstances justified for defence.
predicates.death_caused_without_premeditation_or_ex: The accused caused death without premeditation and without intending to cause more harm than was necessary for defence.

issues.definition: When a person responding to an immediate threat exceeds the right of private defence and causes death without premeditation or an intention to cause more harm than necessary, a culpable-homicide conviction may stand.

issues.legal_issue: The special protection against imprisonment for a person under twenty-one does not apply when the offence of which that person is found guilty is punishable with imprisonment for life.
material_facts: The accused was under twenty-one years of age.
He was found guilty under Section 304 Part I of the Indian Penal Code, an offence punishable with imprisonment for life.
The accused sought the benefit of Section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958, and argued that the offence should instead be treated under Section 304 Part II to make that protection available.
issues.conclusion: Section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act did not apply because the offence of which the accused was found guilty was punishable with imprisonment for life; the sentence was maintained.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 applies to a person under twenty-one found guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment but not with imprisonment for life. The Court held that the offence of conviction was punishable with imprisonment for life and that the conviction could not be changed to attract Section 6. No earlier cases were cited on this issue.

predicates.sentencing_or_probation_issue: The proceeding concerns whether a young offender may receive special probation protection at sentencing.
predicates.offender_under_twenty_one: The offender was younger than twenty-one when found guilty.
predicates.offence_punishable_with_life_imprisonmen: The offence of which the offender was found guilty is punishable with imprisonment for life.

issues.definition: Special youth probation protection is unavailable when an offender under twenty-one is found guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for life.
